summary:
Two criminal-law regimes apply across the Palestinian Territories, and the split between them determines what a trans visitor faces. In the West Bank the governing text is the Jordanian Penal Code No. 16 of 1960, which carried forward Jordan's 1951 revision removing offences covering consensual private sexual conduct, so no provision of that code criminalises consensual same-sex acts. In Gaza the Criminal Code Ordinance No. 74 of 1936 is treated as the operative text by the monitors that report it in force: section 152(2) punishes consensual same-sex "carnal knowledge" by up to ten years' imprisonment, section 152(2)(b) covers carnal knowledge against the law of nature on the same ten-year scale, and section 152(1)(c) sets up to fourteen years for sodomy with a child under sixteen.

Whether the 1936 ordinance is actually in force in Gaza is contested inside the record. The Human Dignity Trust and Human Rights Watch hold it in force, Amnesty International does not report same-sex acts as illegal there, and the legal commentator Anis F. Kassim has argued the text can be read as permitting homosexuality. CAIRO 51 also lists the ordinance as in force in Gaza.

The Palestinian Authority has legislated neither for nor against homosexuality. A 2003 draft Palestinian penal code would have criminalised adult consensual same-sex conduct, with up to five years for male-male sodomy, and whether that draft was ever implemented is not known.

Nothing in the record prohibits trans identity as such in either territory. CAIRO 51 states that the 1936 ordinance is silent on trans identities but reaches trans people through public-morality provisions. A human-rights database compiled by Equaldex sets out no legal gender recognition provisions and no broad legal protections from discrimination for LGBTIQ+ people in the Palestinian Territories, which leaves a trans visitor without a recognised route to change identity documents and without a statutory non-discrimination complaint to invoke.

Formal legality does not describe enforcement. Shaul Ganon of the Israeli-based gay rights group Aguda states that Palestinian Authority police have arrested and tortured gay Palestinians, that the stated ground for persecution is usually a collaboration charge, and that he knows of two cases tried explicitly for homosexuality in the three years preceding his statement. The source gives no date for that statement, so the period cannot be fixed. Ganon links the deterioration to the intifada period, after which police increasingly enforced Islamic law, and states that since then it has been impossible to be openly gay in Palestinian Authority areas. He also describes gay Palestinians blackmailed into acting as informants for Israeli security services.

Public organising has drawn an official ban. Palestinian Authority police prohibited LGBTQ activity by the queer cultural organisation al-Qaws, after which the foundation received a wave of hate messages that activists said posed a serious threat to the gay community. No date is given for the police action in the source.

Family and social exposure carries the practical risk. Legal Clarity states that social and family persecution makes the reality harsher than the formal law, and a joint statement of 11 June 2018 by Human Rights Watch, the Women's Centre for Legal Aid and Counselling and Equality Now reports that twelve Palestinian women identifying as lesbian, bisexual or queer described discrimination and abuse in public and family settings. That is a twelve-person, women-only sample with a 2018 reporting window. The record contains no trans-specific survey and no count of transphobic incidents carrying a date or a period, so the frequency of such incidents cannot be established from this material.

HIV care is a documented access problem. Antiretroviral therapy is described as interrupted for HIV-positive queer people because medication is limited and social stigma is high, and comprehensive epidemiological surveillance is lacking. Only 98 HIV/AIDS cases were officially registered across the Palestinian Territories between 1988 and 2017, comprising 79 people with AIDS and 19 HIV-positive people, a total the source says is likely far below the true figure because taboos hinder data collection. Since October 2023 the collapse of Gaza's healthcare system together with Israeli blockades has made life-saving HIV medication especially difficult to obtain there.
tangentialFactors:
Public acceptance of homosexuality in Palestine is ranked 130th on the Global Acceptance Index, which records very little change over the decade from 2010 to 2020. The index measures social acceptance rather than legal status or enforcement, and its measurement window closed in 2020.

The applicable texts descend from a layered set of Ottoman, British, Jordanian, Egyptian and Israeli legal legacies, and neighbouring state Israel stopped applying the British Mandate criminal code in 1977. Decriminalisation in the West Bank therefore follows from a neighbouring jurisdiction's 1951 revision of that lineage rather than from any Palestinian legislation.

Flight out of the territories is documented as a response to the conditions above: some 90 LGBT Palestinians received temporary permits to seek refuge in Israel after fleeing violence, and Israel began issuing work permits to gay Palestinians granted asylum and to those fleeing domestic violence only in June 2022.

The record describes discrimination and abuse against queer Palestinians rather than isolating a trans-specific pattern, and the one quantitative violence figure it carries is a raw count of two prosecutions over an undated three-year window with no population denominator. It cannot be compared against a general rate.
localsOnly:
The Palestinian Authority has legislated neither for nor against homosexuality, so residents hold no domestic statute defining their position, and the 2003 draft penal code that would have imposed up to five years for male-male sodomy remains of unknown status.

Equaldex sets out no legal gender recognition provisions for residents of the Palestinian Territories and no broad legal protections from discrimination for LGBTIQ+ people, which means changing a marker or bringing a discrimination claim has no sourced domestic legal pathway.

Islamist actors contest LGBTQ content in education and youth spaces. The Palestinian Mujahideen Movement and the Rightly-Guided Caliphs Assembly criticised UNRWA for promoting what they describe as un-Islamic values including LGBTQ issues, and the Islamic Movement in Israel opposed a conversion therapy ban in that state; the activist Maisan Hamdan notes that the movement's sole stated aim is Palestine's liberation without LGBTQ inclusion.

Civil society groups protecting women and children are described as vulnerable to attack in Gaza. Palestinian queer organisations are reported as operating from within Israel, and statelessness is cited as a structural condition of Palestinian LGBTQ life.

HIV surveillance for residents rests on a registered total of 98 cases between 1988 and 2017, with taboos said to hinder data collection, and Gaza's health system has been in collapse since October 2023.
outOfScopeNotes:
Applicability of the 1936 Criminal Code Ordinance in Gaza is unresolved within the source set: The Human Dignity Trust and Human Rights Watch hold it in force, Amnesty International does not report same-sex acts as illegal there, and Anis F. Kassim argues it can be read as permitting homosexuality. No source settles the question.

Whether the 2003 draft Palestinian penal code was implemented is not sourced, and the record does not indicate whether any successor draft is pending or in force.

Three items carry missing or relative dates: the Palestinian Authority police action against al-Qaws is undated; Shaul Ganon's reference to two explicit homosexuality prosecutions covers "the last three years" of an unstated base date; and the transphobic threats and attacks referenced in the record carry no dates or counts at all. No most-recent documented instance can therefore be dated.

No trans-specific violence figure with a denominator appears anywhere in the record, so no comparison between a trans homicide or assault rate and the general rate can be made, and none is asserted.

Not sourced in this material: entry and visa procedure, gender markers on passports or identity documents, airport or checkpoint screening practices, treatment of binders, packers or breast forms, bathroom and facility access, detention placement by gender, hate-crime provisions or their enforcement, medical screening on arrival, and recognition of a partner or marriage. None of these can be confirmed or excluded from the inventory.

The claim that the Palestinian Authority is a non-signatory to key treaties does not name the treaties concerned, so the scope of the protection gap is unresolved.
